title: Juice Uses Earth’s Gravity on Its Way to Jupiter
summary:
The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, called Juice, passed Earth on September 28, 2026. Earth’s gravity helped change its path toward Jupiter. This used very little fuel.

The move is called a gravity assist. A planet’s gravity can change a spacecraft’s speed and direction. Juice turned by 20 degrees and gained 3.5 kilometres per second in speed.

At its closest point, Juice was 8,640 kilometres above the Indian Ocean. Its cameras took pictures as it passed.

The team planned carefully. In the four weeks before the visit, controllers made just one small change to Juice’s path. They had planned six possible chances to make changes.

Angela Dietz, Juice’s spacecraft operations manager, said this planning helped save fuel. The saved fuel leaves more for studying Jupiter’s icy moons.

Scientists also checked Juice’s instruments, the tools it uses to take measurements. Checking and adjusting these tools is called calibration. Earth was useful for these tests because scientists know it well.

Teams spent months planning tests with the groups responsible for Juice’s 10 scientific instruments. They had to share the spacecraft’s time, power and other resources.

Juice project scientist Claire Vallat said the journey gives only a few chances to test the tools in conditions scientists understand well. In Earth’s shadow, Juice used only battery power. Teams chose tests that would help prepare the tools for Jupiter.

Juice also spent several days in Earth’s magnetotail. This is the long part of Earth’s magnetic field that reaches away from the Sun.

Juice is scheduled to pass Jupiter’s moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa 35 times in total. Planning began years ago. Its Europa visits are expected in the early 2030s.

The Earth visit was a practice run. It helped scientists learn how the tools work in space and prepare to study future measurements. Controllers are continuing to track Juice closely through October 10.
why_it_matters: Saving fuel leaves more for studying Jupiter’s icy moons. Testing the tools near Earth also helps scientists prepare for future measurements.
